article_paragraphs: With all the fluids modern cars require, it's only natural to wonder whether one lubricant can handle multiple duties. Scratch hypoid gear oil off the list if you want the engine or most transmissions to keep functioning properly. We'll get to the reason shortly, but let's first explain how hypoid gearsets work. These gears, located in the differential between the rear (or sometimes front) wheels, are common on tow-oriented pickups and body-on-frame SUVs. Some all-wheel-drive vehicles also have a hypoid gear setup in the power transfer unit, which directs power back to the rear wheels.

Originally called a hyperboloidal gear, hypoid is the modernized term for a setup where the pinion gear meets the ring gear offset from the center. The driveshaft sits below, lowering the center of gravity and opening up more floor space. However, the gear teeth rub against each other in a sliding motion that squeezes the lubricant away from the teeth, leaving the metal surfaces without a full oil film between them (known as boundary lubrication). A specialized lubricant with EP (extreme pressure) additives inside the oil protects the exposed metal once the oil film between the gear teeth is squeezed out. This kind of gear oil meant for hypoid differentials typically carries the American Petroleum Institute (API) GL-5 designation. Let's look at how it's different.

Two of the most important tasks of engine oil include lubricating the internal moving parts and managing the byproducts of the combustion process. Proper oil pressure maintains a full film on most moving parts, but some components, like the camshaft and lifters, may still have boundary conditions. Engine oil deals with these areas with milder anti-wear additives, such as ZDDP (zinc dialkyl dithiophosphate), instead of the heavy EP formulations found in gear oil. Simply put, the EP additives in gear oil aren't made for use inside an engine. These formulations start to become corrosive to some metals found inside the engine at about 200 degrees Fahrenheit. In addition, the use of phosphorus-based additives in engine oil is kept to a minimum to prevent catalytic converter damage.

Meanwhile, detergents and dispersants in engine oil control soot and sludge buildup inside the powerplant. Differentials don't have to deal with these contaminants. Instead, differential gear oil has to maintain a thin layer of lubrication between the gears, whether the vehicle is operating normally, driving under load, or pulling a heavy trailer. Engine oil lacks the necessary EP additives that support this. Oil thickness is also worth mentioning. Each fluid uses different SAE scales: J300 for engine oil and J306 for gear oil. So the numbers don't line up. For example, a 90 viscosity-grade gear oil falls in roughly the same thickness range as SAE 40 and 50 engine oils, not twice as thick. Nonetheless, modern engines are designed to use lighter-weight oils than much heavier gear oil.

Swapping gear oil for transmission fluid, or vice versa, may seem possible, since hypoid differentials and manual transmissions are both complex collections of gears. However, shift-it-yourself gearboxes mostly use helical gears that have far less sliding than the hypoid gears used in most standalone differentials. You'll also find that many manual transmissions require a GL-4 lubricant, which has about half the EP additives of a GL-5 oil.

An EP-heavy GL-5 lubricant relies on sulfur-phosphorus additives to provide protection. Yet this formulation can corrode the brass synchronizers used in many manual transmissions, and the risk worsens at higher temperatures. Other brass and bronze (yellow metal) components can also be at risk with a GL-5 oil. Friction also comes into play, as synchronizers need grip before engaging a gear. Many differential oils are formulated to be slippery, which can cause poor shifting in manuals not designed to work with GL-5 oils.

Of course, nothing is always black and white in the car world. Some cars with manual gearboxes call for GL-5 transmission lubrication. Examples include certain Subaru models. Aftermarket suppliers also make GL-5 gear oil specifically for manual transmission applications. Keep in mind that manual and automatic transmission fluids aren't interchangeable .

title: Why US GP has left Verstappen and Hadjar furious with Red Bull
raw_summary: Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar let rip at Red Bull after Formula 1's United States Grand Prix for a series of avoidable problems that left them unable to fully capitalise on the potential of their car. Things went wrong at the start as Verstappen and Hadjar in particular made poor getaways from second and third on the grid.

Things went wrong at the start as Verstappen and Hadjar in particular made poor getaways from second and third on the grid.
article_paragraphs: Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar let rip at Red Bull after Formula 1's United States Grand Prix for a series of avoidable problems that left them unable to fully capitalise on the potential of their car.
Things went wrong at the start as Verstappen and Hadjar in particular made poor getaways from second and third on the grid.

The pair were then hampered throughout the race by radio problems that made communication with the pitwall difficult, while Verstappen was annoyed about the choice of a two-stop strategy that left the door open for the one-stopping Kimi Antonelli to take a dominant win.

Despite a radio message from team principal Laurent Mekies immediately after the chequered flag confessing the team had "a few things to tidy up", it was clear that frustrations were high in the cockpit.
In a bleak post-race radio message after taking the chequered flag in third, Verstappen said: "Terrible: the pace, the wrong tyre, sh** pitstop, sh** engine braking. Nothing worked."

Speaking to Viaplay after the race about whether he agreed on the strategy call in committing to softs for the second stint when the harder compounds appeared to be in play, Verstappen said: "No, it wasn't agreed upon. That's why I don't get it. Then everyone would know we're doing a two-stop."

Later on, referencing struggles with balance and engine braking that were not helped by the ongoing radio problems, Verstappen sarcastically told the media: "Maybe we just start communicating in sign language. It's probably cheaper as well.
Hadjar was even angrier, as he suggested that Red Bull needed a new clutch design because of the repeated weak starts.

title: Audi Will Invest $4 Billion To Build A Factory In Georgia
raw_summary: Audi will invest about $4 billion to build a large factory in Georgia, making it the German brand's first production plant in the United States. The company has been evaluating a local production facility for well over a year in response to the Trump administration's tariffs and has finally decided it's the right time to build it. Unlike rival BMW, which builds thousands of vehicles in the U.S., Audi produces all the vehicles it sells locally in overseas factories, meaning they're subject to tariffs. These tariffs cost Audi $1.4 billion last year alone, and it can't absorb those costs forever. The new plant, set to commence construction next year, will have an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles, with production scheduled to start in the early 2030s.

These tariffs cost Audi $1.4 billion last year alone, and it can't absorb those costs forever. The new plant, set to commence construction next year, will have an annual capacity of up to 200,000 vehicles, with production scheduled to start in the early 2030s.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced the plant during a campaign rally in Georgia and even brought Audi's Chairman of the Board of Management, Gernot Döllner, onto the stage. Audi says it will build premium SUVs at the new plant and believes it will "unlock significant growth potential in one of the world's most important premium markets." It also says the site will help establish North America as the third major pillar of its global production network alongside Europe and China.

The Middle Georgia Mega Site will create approximately 4,500 jobs and also generate new opportunities among suppliers, training partners, and service providers. President Trump has cited his tariffs as sparking a resurgence in U.S. manufacturing and, during his speech in Georgia, claimed that approximately $40 billion has been invested in the nation's automotive industry, creating 30,000 new jobs.

"We have much greater ambitions for Audi in America," Döllner said. "The United States is one of the world's most important premium markets, and we have not yet realized our full potential. We are determined to change that — with premium products, a stronger brand and a competitive local production base. This is about building a stronger Audi business in America — not only about building a factory."

Audi did not specify which models it will build at the factory. However, Reuters reports they will include the Q7, Q8, and the all-new Q9 , which was displayed at the rally in Georgia over the weekend. It has also been reported that Audi could build up to 25,000 vehicles at Scout's planned South Carolina factory.

"Building a new plant from the ground up allows us to rethink manufacturing from day one," added Audi board member for Production and Logistics, Gerd Walker. "We can design highly efficient and flexible production processes, integrate advanced technologies and develop a strong local supplier network. Our ambition is to establish a benchmark for premium manufacturing that strengthens Audi's global production network."

The new Georgia factory won't only give Audi an answer to BMW's local production presence. Mercedes-Benz also operates a major manufacturing hub in Alabama. Recent investments at this site will increase annual production up to 340,000 units. Popular models built here include the Mercedes GLE, GLS, EQE SUV, EQS SUV, Sprinter, and, starting late next year, the GLC.

raw_title: That Time Someone Stole A Hyundai Tucson Holding Both Parents' Ashes The Night Before A Funeral
title: That Time Someone Stole A Hyundai Tucson Holding Both Parents' Ashes The Night Before A Funeral
raw_summary: There's been a dramatic drop-off in car thefts over the past two years, with the number of stolen cars falling 17% in 2024 from 2023, and another 23% in 2025. In fact, those were the two largest yearly declines in the past four decades. On the other hand, 2023 marked the highest number of stolen cars in the past four decades — and that included a 2016 Hyundai Tucson owned by Kimberly Magnusson. In 2023, car thieves not only took irreplaceable mementos of her deceased parents, including her father's military service flag, but her parents' actual remains as well. Furthermore, this theft occurred the night before the funeral. Magnusson, who drove up from Texas, was in Greeley, Colorado, for the funeral when the theft occurred. The good news is that everything was eventually found and returned. The bad news is that the recovery happened weeks after the funeral was over, and the Tucson's interior had suffered ignition, steering column, and door lock damage.

In fact, those were the two largest yearly declines in the past four decades. On the other hand, 2023 marked the highest number of stolen cars in the past four decades — and that included a 2016 Hyundai Tucson owned by Kimberly Magnusson.

In 2023, car thieves not only took irreplaceable mementos of her deceased parents, including her father's military service flag, but her parents' actual remains as well. Furthermore, this theft occurred the night before the funeral. Magnusson, who drove up from Texas, was in Greeley, Colorado, for the funeral when the theft occurred. The good news is that everything was eventually found and returned. The bad news is that the recovery happened weeks after the funeral was over, and the Tucson's interior had suffered ignition, steering column, and door lock damage.

If the U.S. only had the same anti-theft laws that Canada passed years ago , the crime may never have happened. That's because the 2016 Tucson was one of the many vehicles caught up in the Kia Boys fiasco. As you may remember, this was caused by Hyundai's decision not to install engine immobilizers on certain Kia and Hyundai products sold in the United States — but not Canada, where they're legally required. Moreover, despite the automaker's fixes, car theft numbers show that the Hyundai Elantra and Sonata were ranked No. 1 and No. 3, respectively, on the list of most stolen cars of 2025. Hyundai and Kia did see their third straight year of declining thefts in 2025, though.

Even if the Tucson didn't appear in our worst car-theft story for 2025 having a vehicle stolen containing human cremains can be surprisingly common. At least five cases were reported on the internet earlier this year: once in Indianapolis in May, again in Albuquerque in June, another time in Oakland, California, during August, and twice in September (Warren, Michigan, and Chicago).

The obvious risk is that something could happen to the ashes — for example, if a criminal breaks open an urn to see if there are valuables inside and pours out the cremains to check. But there's also another aspect to consider. Human cremains should be stored in a dry area with stable temperatures. Now, it's not because they'll decompose or anything like that. After cremation, mostly all that's left is inorganic materials like calcium phosphate and other mineral salts. Bacteria and other microbes generally won't grow on that kind of stuff. But the ashes can be affected by moisture. In fact, if human cremains get wet, they'll clump together in what's been described as a thick, chunky paste. You can dry the material out and re-pulverize it, but the task probably wouldn't be anyone's idea of fun.

Additionally, anything left out in your car — from a fancy funeral urn to a nondescript temporary container — can be a temptation for car thieves. And they won't be fooled if you hide it under a blanket or jacket, or tuck it under a seat. According to some law enforcement agencies, the safest place to store loose items is your car's trunk.

raw_title: Alonso calls 33% of the F1 grid 'low quality'
title: Alonso calls 33% of the F1 grid 'low quality
raw_summary: Fernando Alonso has taken aim at Alex Albon following their collision on lap one of the United States Grand Prix, calling him part of a lower-third of the Formula 1 grid where "the quality of the drivers" is "very low". Albon dived to the inside of Alonso, who had Esteban Ocon's Haas on his outside, but made contact that Albon said damaged his Williams's front wing and that stripped the left-hand bargeboard from Alonso's Aston Martin. Alonso described this variously as having left him with "half a car" and damage that was costing him "half a second or more" per lap, and pondered "I don't know how we kept on going and how we were semi-competitive". And after the race he took issue with Albon's move, which was not penalised by the F1 stewards. "I think when you start at the back there is this risk always," said Alonso, who finished a lapped 16th following a slow second stop to change his front wing. "I think the quality of the drivers in the lower third of the grid is very low, as we saw today with Alex. "So I think we need to improve the car and start a little bit higher up." Asked by F1 TV for his view on the incident, Alonso said that "Albon forgot that corner 11 was there and he had to turn left" and reiterated his point about the quality of drivers in the bottom third of the grid being "low". Alonso claimed afterwards he thought it was "by far" his best race of the season and that without the contact he could have finished in the points on merit. He underlined this later by quipping in a question about Aston Martin's performance level relative to Williams, which is five points ahead in the battle for ninth in the constructors' championship, that "we could have scored points today and maybe get close in the constructors' championship, but they made sure that we didn't have any chance". Those Alonso quotes were not put directly to Albon, but he likened their battles in the race - Alonso did pass Albon again late on, after a slow second pitstop where his front wing was changed - to the kind of Ford Mustang versus Mini battle seen in historic races at Goodwood. He added that "it's always fun to race Fernando", who is "strong, but he's fair always" before adding: "Maybe he thought I was a bit over the edge, I don't know - I'm sure I'll find out soon. But I had a good amount of fun." Albon said of their clash: "It felt like there was a car on the right side of Fernando [Ocon] and he gave Fernando enough space as if he thought there was only one car on his inside but then I was on the inside of Fernando so then I think it pinched and I tried to get out of the way and get on the kerb but I didn't make all of it.

Those Alonso quotes were not put directly to Albon, but he likened their battles in the race - Alonso did pass Albon again late on, after a slow second pitstop where his front wing was changed - to the kind of Ford Mustang versus Mini battle seen in historic races at Goodwood. He added that "it's always fun to race Fernando", who is "strong, but he's fair always" before adding: "Maybe he thought I was a bit over the edge, I don't know - I'm sure I'll find out soon. But I had a good amount of fun."

Albon said of their clash: "It felt like there was a car on the right side of Fernando [Ocon] and he gave Fernando enough space as if he thought there was only one car on his inside but then I was on the inside of Fernando so then I think it pinched and I tried to get out of the way and get on the kerb but I didn't make all of it.
"So I imagine he got damage, I know I got damage, driving around with a broken wing for the race."

Albon dived to the inside of Alonso, who had Esteban Ocon's Haas on his outside, but made contact that Albon said damaged his Williams's front wing and that stripped the left-hand bargeboard from Alonso's Aston Martin.

title: 7 Of The Most Powerful JDM Engines Ever Made
raw_summary: In 1989 one of the odder bits of automotive history happened in Japan. Known as the Japanese Gentlemen's Agreement , the JAMA (Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association) agreed that they would limit their vehicles to 280 horsepower. This was at a time when automotive deaths in Japan were very high, and the thought was this would prevent a horsepower war and, in turn, save lives. Nice thought. Did the automakers stick to this agreement? On paper, yes. Until about 2004, vehicles from Japan topped out at 280 hp. The Skyline GT-R? 280 hp. The Honda NSX? 280 hp. The Toyota Supra? You guessed it, "only" 280 hp. This handshake deal lasted until the early 2000's when the brave Honda/Acura Legend quietly broke the non-binding agreement and opened it up for the other manufacturers to quit pretending. Plus by this point, improved vehicle safety equipment had proven its value. Vehicles got safer, and fewer folks died as a result of car wrecks. Hooray!

article_paragraphs: In 1989 one of the odder bits of automotive history happened in Japan. Known as the Japanese Gentlemen's Agreement , the JAMA (Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association) agreed that they would limit their vehicles to 280 horsepower. This was at a time when automotive deaths in Japan were very high, and the thought was this would prevent a horsepower war and, in turn, save lives. Nice thought.

Did the automakers stick to this agreement? On paper, yes. Until about 2004, vehicles from Japan topped out at 280 hp. The Skyline GT-R? 280 hp. The Honda NSX? 280 hp. The Toyota Supra? You guessed it, "only" 280 hp. This handshake deal lasted until the early 2000's when the brave Honda/Acura Legend quietly broke the non-binding agreement and opened it up for the other manufacturers to quit pretending. Plus by this point, improved vehicle safety equipment had proven its value. Vehicles got safer, and fewer folks died as a result of car wrecks. Hooray!

That clears the way for us to have our very own horsepower war. Here are seven of the most powerful JDM internal combustion engines ever put into production, plus one honorable mention. It was tricky getting real numbers and impossible to know every JDM engine out there, so let us know what we missed. Also if an engine had a high horsepower brethren in the same engine family that could have made the list, we showcased the most powerful engine of the fam in order to make the list not just Toyota and Nissan.

"With a purposeful grimace and a terrible sound" sang Blue Oyster Cult on their 1977 hit Godzilla. While this song really has nothing to do with Nissan or the GT-R, it does pop into the head of car enthusiasts of a certain age when they think about the word "Godzilla." We're speaking, obviously, of the Nissan GT-R and the VR38DETT that makes this monster growl. The VR38DETT is a twin-turbocharged Dual-Overhead Camshaft (DOHC) 3.9-liter V6 engine that powers the legendary Nissan R35 GT-R. Starting in 2007, a small team of "Takumi," or master builders, hand-built these engines.. In the "normal" GT-R they pushed out a respectable 565 hp and 467 pound-feet of torque. For the NISMO version, it cranked out 600 hp at 6,800 rpm and 481 lb-ft of torque. Go go, indeed.

While the GT-R is the only production vehicle the engine made it into, over the years it had a cameo in a couple wild concepts, notably the bonkers Juke-R , which went on sale for $600,000 . The engine lasted a solid 19 years before it and the GT-R were officially retired from production in 2024.

Toyota chairman, Akio Toyoda had dreams of being a racecar driver. He was able to secretly pursue this under the moniker Morizo and race at the Nürburgring, but there was a problem: at that time, Toyota didn't make any cars that were competitive, so he got passed often. This frustrated Morizo and started him on the path to make cars that could compete. The peak of this goal was the Lexus LFA, which was built to be a supercar to rival the best in the world.

To be the best, the LFA needed an amazing engine, and in 2009 the 1LR-GUE was born. Developed in cooperation with Yamaha, this powerhouse is a 552-560 hp liquid-cooled 4-stroke DOHC 4.8-liter V10 that sits at a 72-degree V-angle. Built to be incredibly high revving, it goes from idle to its 9000 rpm redline in just 0.6 seconds—so fast that an analog tachometer couldn't keep up, so they had to go digital. This shot the LFA from 0-60 mph in a scant 3.6 seconds, maxing out at a 202 mph top speed.These specs demonstrate how quick the car is, but it doesn't capture how fantastic it sounds doing it. Some call it "the roar of an angel," MotorTrend calls it "by far one of the most beautiful-sounding cars ever built." Yamaha specifically engineered the engine to achieve that rich, screaming, F1-like sound. The LFA had a short 2-year production run, with just 500 units built before it was discontinued in 2012.

While the LFA was winning over the hearts, minds, and ears of enthusiasts everywhere, it was only the beginning of the story. The Lexus F line of high-performance vehicles spread out the awesome sauce across the product line. The heart of the F line is the 2UR-GSE, a naturally aspirated DOHC 5-liter V8. Output varied across its lifespan and application, but at its peak it put out 472 hp and 395 lb-ft of torque.

title: 7 Cars And Trucks That Have Some Of The Worst MPG Ratings Ever
raw_summary: While some countries are out there selling gas for less than $2 a gallon , in the U.S., we're seeing prices sitting near the $5 mark, so it's worth highlighting the models that burn through fuel at record rates. Now, of course, some historic vehicles with aircraft-powered racing machines and other such rare antique engines will be laughably inefficient, but the focus here is actually on more modern machinery. The sort of cars you might actually stand a chance of seeing one day, like the Dodge Ram SRT-10, and its modern successor, the Ram 1500 TRX. To inject a little excitement, we've also thrown in some significant and woefully inefficient supercars, like Lamborghini's angular Countach and the sixteen-cylinder Bugatti Veyron.

Now, of course, some historic vehicles with aircraft-powered racing machines and other such rare antique engines will be laughably inefficient, but the focus here is actually on more modern machinery. The sort of cars you might actually stand a chance of seeing one day, like the Dodge Ram SRT-10, and its modern successor, the Ram 1500 TRX. To inject a little excitement, we've also thrown in some significant and woefully inefficient supercars, like Lamborghini's angular Countach and the sixteen-cylinder Bugatti Veyron.

It's worth noting that all of these cars and trucks do have their uses. We aren't claiming they are useless and should be avoided just because of their poor fuel economy. Still, anyone scared of current fuel prices should steer well clear. Listed in order of their efficiency, with the most "impressive" featured first, here are our seven cars and trucks with some of the worst mpg ratings.

The 2021 Hellcat-powered Ram 1500 TRX has some serious off-road pedigree. A 702-horsepower supercharged V8 enables this TRX to dart from 0 to 60 mph in just 3.7 seconds, while Bilstein remote-reservoir dampers, an electronic-locking rear diff, and 35-inch all-terrain tires ensure it's capable when the going gets tough.

Blistered wide arches see the TRX sitting a full 8 inches wider than standard 1500 models. While the wide arches themselves don't significantly increase weight, the wider mechanical components underneath help increase its base curb weight to a hefty 6,396 pounds. Piece all that info together — supercharged V8, massive tires, and a robust curb weight — and it should come as no surprise that the TRX finds itself on our list of vehicles with the worst fuel economy.

The EPA provides a combined rating of just 12 mpg, consisting of a 10 mpg rating around town and 14 mpg on the highway. However, in independent testing, the TRX has actually performed even less admirably than this, with as little as 9 mpg reported. Not the wisest choice for those who fear rising fuel prices.

The Ferrari Enzo is about as far removed from a TRX as one could possibly get, sporting minuscule ground clearance, low-profile performance tires, and a naturally aspirated 6.0-liter V12. Yet, unsurprisingly, the two vehicles share something in common: woeful fuel economy.

Of course, a multi-million-dollar supercar is never going to be a Prius rival, but it's worth taking a look at just how inefficient the Enzo's 6.0-liter V12 is. Its EPA-provided rating is 12 mpg on the highway, and just 7 mpg around town, for a combined score of just 8 mpg. Independent testing sees the Enzo achieve 11 mpg, so actually better than the EPA suggests. Clearly, though, in addition to needing around $8 million in the bank to buy one in the first place, wannabe Enzo owners will also need to assign a decent portion of their net worth to actually keeping the thing fueled up. Those on a budget could always opt for a Fiero-based Enzo 'replica' instead, but the embarrassment of being seen in such a monstrosity likely outweighs any financial benefits there are to be had.

raw_title: America Needs More Types Of Driver's Licenses, Not Just Better Driver's Ed
title: America Needs More Types Of Driver's Licenses, Not Just Better Driver's Ed
raw_summary: As an auto journalist , I have more track experience than at least 99% of U.S. drivers, due purely to the fact that I've been on the track at all . In fact, I usually get out there at least a couple of times a year. Your average enthusiast probably doesn't do that, and your average driver in the U.S. definitely doesn't. Most recently, Michelin invited me to attend the AMG Experience at Road Atlanta — sorry, Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta — and while several folks there definitely knew what they were doing, let's just say I left even more convinced that America needs different tiers of drivers' licenses. Not everyone who buys an AMG necessarily plans to flog it like a race car, but still, it was remarkable watching a few people struggle to do what the instructor was telling them, much less turn in a quick-ish lap time. At an event they were attending because they'd recently bought a new AMG. Wealthy, older men buying cars with capabilities that exceed their driving skills isn't anything new, and that experience could have gotten several of them hooked on real driving. Besides, it's not like younger enthusiasts don't love buying performance cars they can't handle, too. I honestly wish they didn't, if only so every Cars & Coffee wasn't 65% jokes about the Ford Mustang .

article_paragraphs: As an auto journalist , I have more track experience than at least 99% of U.S. drivers, due purely to the fact that I've been on the track at all . In fact, I usually get out there at least a couple of times a year. Your average enthusiast probably doesn't do that, and your average driver in the U.S. definitely doesn't. Most recently, Michelin invited me to attend the AMG Experience at Road Atlanta — sorry, Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta — and while several folks there definitely knew what they were doing, let's just say I left even more convinced that America needs different tiers of drivers' licenses.

Not everyone who buys an AMG necessarily plans to flog it like a race car, but still, it was remarkable watching a few people struggle to do what the instructor was telling them, much less turn in a quick-ish lap time. At an event they were attending because they'd recently bought a new AMG. Wealthy, older men buying cars with capabilities that exceed their driving skills isn't anything new, and that experience could have gotten several of them hooked on real driving. Besides, it's not like younger enthusiasts don't love buying performance cars they can't handle, too. I honestly wish they didn't, if only so every Cars & Coffee wasn't 65% jokes about the Ford Mustang .

In some ways, it's cool that you can pretty much buy any car you want as long as you have a license or permit and the money for it, but we can all think of at least a few downsides to that system. College kids can afford Dodge Chargers with V8s. High school sophomores with budgets that barely cover cars that run, drive, and start almost every time can just buy heavily depreciated liter bikes instead. And there's nothing stopping your clumsiest, most scatterbrained buddy from buying a Chevrolet Silverado 2500HD. But things could be different if the U.S. required people to get different licenses in order to drive different vehicles.

While most people probably assume a basic U.S. driver's license lets them drive anything they want, that's definitely not true. You can't drive a tractor-trailer without a commercial driver's license, and if you want a motorcycle, you have to get a motorcycle license. Technically, you don't need a license to drive either on private land, but we're talking about public roads here. You know, the roads where you might hurt my nieces and nephews if you crash like an idiot.

America's a big country, so a few folks will probably argue that anyone should be able to drive a big rig or a motorcycle if they want, without any government interference and licensing . They probably also think every road should be a toll road because they're all operated by private companies, and they really don't want you checking their browser histories. Creepy internet weirdos aside, though, the rest of us can probably all agree it makes sense that riding a motorcycle is a different skill than driving, and driving a giant truck towing a heavy load isn't quite the same as driving a Honda Civic to Popeyes. Different types of vehicles require different skills, and testing those skills means different licenses.

No matter how long you've driven a car, you're no closer to knowing how to ride a motorcycle than anyone with less driving experience. And while another driver could probably get a Silverado 3500 going no problem, do they know how to turn with a 30,000 pound trailer? Can they recover safely if the trailer starts to lean a little too much? Would you trust a high schooler to do either, even if they've watched their parents do both for years? Of course not. We test different skills and hand out different licenses because it keeps you, me, and our loved ones safer. And while we can't account for everything, it at least makes sense to put some guardrails up.

I'm just spitballing here, so don't get too hung up in the specifics, but what about a second motorcycle license for anything over 500cc? A license that slots below the CDL for anyone who wants to tow more than, say, a few thousand pounds? Oh, and if it runs the Nürburgring in less than 8:30, you should probably get a special license for that, too. I also love the idea of a medium-speed license that lets you drive Medium-Speed Vehicles, affordable cars that are more substantial than the Fiat Topolino and capable of, say, 45 mph (compared to some previous suggestions, I'm being generous).

The tests would have to be hard enough that passing would require demonstrating real skill, and experts should probably fine-tune my ideas, but they at least have potential. And that's just the beginning. We could add even more licenses, and they don't necessarily have to involve driving skills. Maybe if you want to drive a vintage car, you have to sit through a bunch of videos showing all the ways cutting corners and shoddy work can come back to bite you (followed, of course, by an hour of crash videos showing vintage cars being destroyed by modern vehicles). Normies would probably get scared off, but true enthusiasts would love spending a few hours watching idiots' mistakes come back to bite them and some cool crash videos.

On September 30, 2026, Volkswagen Group announced it was terminating many of the wage provisions it agreed to in December, 2024 with IG Metall, the union that represents many of Volkswagen’s workers. According to Reuters , the terminated provisions included wage agreements that cover more than 100,000 workers at Volkswagen’s primary factories in Germany. Those agreements govern such things as working hours and holiday pay, provisions that IG Metal sees as benefits it won for workers after long and often contentious negotiations with the company.

The last time Volkswagen cancelled parts of its collective bargaining framework with the ​union was in September, 2024. That triggered ​a wave of strikes ⁠that culminated in a landmark labor deal in December, 2024 that included 35,000 job cuts. Part of that agreement provided either side could revisit the terms of the agreement if there was a material change in circumstances.

The company says its deteriorating finances justify its decision to cancel the wage provisions previously agreed to. Human resources chief Arne Meiswinkel said management was acting to ensure the company ​remains fit for the future. “We must continue to work on our cost structures,” he said. Terminating the agreements “gives us room to negotiate ‌so that ⁠we can then agree on the necessary measures.”

Despite that justification by the company, the union and the workers are furious. IG Metall representative Thorsten Groeger thundered, “This is a despicable blow to the workforce. We will not accept this. Anyone who tries to reach into the employees’ pockets must ​expect a fight.”

IG Metall is contractually bound not to strike the company until January 1, 2027, but it is rattling its sabers and warning that strikes will be starting as soon as that deadline passes if the company’s plan not to honor the 2024 agreement is not rescinded by October 31. “We are giving the company until the end of October to withdraw this notice of ​termination,” Thorsten Groeger said in Hanover, where unions and management met for a fresh round of talks last week. “Otherwise a massive process will be set in motion which, let me make this clear, will pave the way for industrial action at Volkswagen.”

“The economic situation has deteriorated dramatically since the collective bargaining agreement for the future was concluded in 2024. raw_title: Antonelli on the brink of first F1 title after crushing US GP win
title: Antonelli on the brink of first F1 title after crushing US GP win
raw_summary: Kimi Antonelli made a one-stop strategy work to win the United States Grand Prix as mid-race challenges from Mercedes' Formula 1 rivals Red Bull and Ferrari failed to materialise in the final stint. A ninth victory of the season left Antonelli on the brink of becoming the youngest-ever F1 world champion, though the 20-year-old will be forced to wait at least one more weekend as Mercedes team-mate George Russell laboured to eighth while Lewis Hamilton finished fourth. Antonelli ultimately won from the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc and Red Bull's Max Verstappen. They ran in that order at the start, too, Antonelli holding the lead off the line on medium tyres and Leclerc squeezing past Verstappen into Turn 4 as the Red Bull appeared to struggle for traction and/or power on the run downhill out of the first corner. Verstappen had made it back ahead of Leclerc before the end of the first lap, with a move through the first part of the multiple right-hand sequence in the final sector, but Antonelli had already built a buffer of two seconds by this point - an advantage he increased steadily in the first stint before Verstappen opened the pitstop window by stopping at the end of lap 13. That put him on a two-stop strategy - Red Bull electing to put him onto another set of softs - and the offset in stint lengths meant he did end up in the lead once the frontrunners had stopped, albeit with Leclerc bearing down on him and Antonelli closing in quickly too. Midway through the 56-lap race Verstappen complained that he "must have a problem with my car, it's undriveable" while 2.1s ahead of Leclerc, and though he managed to keep the Ferrari behind he subsequently pitted on lap 33/56 to move onto mediums for the final stint - Red Bull choosing to avoid the hard tyre that had worked well on its rivals' cars but not on Isack Hadjar's RB22. Antonelli needed only half a lap more once the Red Bull was out of the way to reclaim the lead by overtaking Leclerc into the Turn 12 braking zone, though Mercedes - committed to a one-stop by at this point, having put Antonelli on hards - still felt the Ferrari, which stopped for a second time to also switch to hard tyres, carried the bigger threat. That proved to be the case; Verstappen struggled to make progress as he caught the McLaren of Lando Norris, and though he did finally make his way through - with a well-judged lunge into Turn 1, when he had looked vulnerable to being passed by Leclerc exiting the final corner - Verstappen held second for only three laps more before Leclerc came through. By this point, it was too late for Leclerc to mount a challenge - with Antonelli's only real headache in the closing laps caused by a virtual safety car called so the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas could be recovered from the side of the track, though Mercedes ultimately opted to keep Antonelli out on track rather than pit him for fresh tyres. The late VSC probably ensured Verstappen kept his podium, as a late charge from Hamilton (who matched Ferrari team-mate's Leclerc strategy) left him one second short of third place. He spent the second half of the race holding off Russell's Mercedes, which had been hamstrung by a five-second penalty served at his pitstop for leaving the track and gaining an advantage while battling Piastri on the opening lap. Bearman tried to claim the door had been closed on him but the stewards instead found him guilty of causing a collision and handed him a penalty, which he served at one of three pitstops inside the first 24 laps - the last of which was ultimately to retire the car.

title: If You Want A Hyundai Tucson With A Manual Transmission, Look For These Years
raw_summary: There's a lot to be said for owning a car with a manual transmission. Beyond a more engaging behind-the-wheel experience, a manual may cost less to repair than an automatic. The vehicle's purchase price may be lower, too. The idea of a stick in a used compact crossover may even appeal to some, but that ship sailed two decades ago for the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4. However, Hyundai kept do-it-yourself shifting alive for much longer in the Tucson. We'll cover the details by looking at the 2005 through 2013 model years for the Tucson, separated by generation. We'll include a breakdown of the applicable powertrains (think base engines), available model-year reliability ratings from Consumer Reports (CR), and other considerations buyers of second-hand Tucsons should be aware of (the infamous Theta II engine issue rears its ugly head).

article_paragraphs: There's a lot to be said for owning a car with a manual transmission. Beyond a more engaging behind-the-wheel experience, a manual may cost less to repair than an automatic. The vehicle's purchase price may be lower, too. The idea of a stick in a used compact crossover may even appeal to some, but that ship sailed two decades ago for the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4. However, Hyundai kept do-it-yourself shifting alive for much longer in the Tucson.

We'll cover the details by looking at the 2005 through 2013 model years for the Tucson, separated by generation. We'll include a breakdown of the applicable powertrains (think base engines), available model-year reliability ratings from Consumer Reports (CR), and other considerations buyers of second-hand Tucsons should be aware of (the infamous Theta II engine issue rears its ugly head).

Ordinarily, we'd include marketplace pricing, but this is hard to do for a Tucson with a stick. As of this writing, a cursory search of dealer listings on Cars.com shows only a couple nationwide, both with fewer than 100,000 miles (well below the average for cars 15 to 20 years old). In other words, anything goes for what you'll pay for a Tucson with a manual transmission, assuming you can find one.

Hyundai launched the Tucson in the U.S. for the 2005 model year, which was also the final year of the second-generation RAV4 and the last RAV4 offered with a stick shift. By 2026 standards, the inaugural Tucson's specs were modest, with a base 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine making 140 horsepower. This unit was exclusive to the entry-level GL trim, as was a five-speed manual transmission. A four-speed automatic gearbox was optional on the GL and standard with the higher-grade GLS and LX, which came with a 2.7-liter V6 engine making 173 horsepower. Front-wheel drive (FWD) was standard, with all-wheel drive (AWD) optional across the trim range. However, on the GL, AWD required the manual transmission.

Hyundai maintained a three-trim lineup with the same engine range throughout the first generation, which ended in 2009, but changed the trim names over the years. For the 2008 and 2009 Tucson, Hyundai dropped AWD availability in the base GLS grade but kept the manual transmission as the base gearbox. By 2009, Hyundai also offered the top-tier Limited trim with the entry-level four-cylinder engine, but it couldn't be equipped with the manual. For the first generation, Consumer Reports only scored the 2006 model year for reliability, giving this Tucson an average rating. Newer examples, like the 2025 Tucson , have higher CR scores.

The second-generation debuted for the 2010 model year and lasted through 2015. However, Hyundai dropped the manual transmission after 2013. The previous generation's stubby presence was replaced with a sleeker exterior and an upscale cabin. Hyundai also made changes under the hood. For 2010, the only engine offered was a 2.4-liter four-cylinder Theta II unit making 170 to 176 horsepower (depending on emissions classification). On the starter GLS trim, a six-speed manual was standard, with a six-speed automatic optional and included with the top-of-the-range Limited edition. Both trims came standard with front-wheel drive, which could be upgraded to all-wheel drive (with the automatic only).

For 2011, the automaker brought back a base GL trim equipped with a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine making 165 horsepower. This powerplant also had Theta II architecture. The front-wheel-drive-only GL came standard with a five-speed manual (one gear less than in 2010), with the six-speed automatic available (and standard on the higher trims). Hyundai continued this arrangement through 2013, dropping the base GL trim and the manual transmission for 2014. The 2011 through 2013 Tucsons received average reliability ratings from Consumer Reports (CR didn't review the 2010 model year).

Hyundai's Theta II engines rank among the worst , but second-generation Tucsons with manual transmissions have an interesting quirk. While the 2010 manual Tucson used the 2.4-liter engine, the 2011 to 2013 manual versions had the 2.0-liter, the less troublesome of the two engines. Hyundai's bearing-related engine replacement campaigns and factory warranty extensions have covered the Tucson's 2.4-liter engine, including the 2010 version paired with a manual. Those programs don't cover the 2011 to 2013 Tucson's 2.0-liter engine. Turbocharged, direct-injected 2.0-liter versions used in the 2013 to 2014 Santa Fe Sport and Sonata were recalled for potential bearing failure caused by manufacturing debris.

raw_title: 4 Ideas To Deck Out Your Car For The Next Halloween Trunk-Or-Treat
title: 4 Ideas To Deck Out Your Car For The Next Halloween Trunk-Or-Treat
raw_summary: For some people, Halloween is no different from any other day, but for others, it is game time. If you're in the second camp, it's time to get your act together for trunk-or-treat. The concept is simple: instead of trudging door to door, kids go car to car in a parking lot, collecting candy from open trunks. Trunk-or-treating works in areas where houses are far apart and gives the whole community an excuse to show up in one place and mingle. It also means your car could become the main attraction, so you need to plan ahead. Nobody remembers the crossover with a bowl of fun-size candy sitting in the cargo area. If you'd rather be the star of the parking lot, we've got a few ideas that won't cost a fortune or eat your whole weekend.

If you'd rather be the star of the parking lot, we've got a few ideas that won't cost a fortune or eat your whole weekend.

Are you the sort of person who looks at a car's front end and sees a face? Some of us are, and that is why we dedicated an entire article to cars with the goofiest faces . Some cars sell the look better than others. For example, the Jeep Wrangler, Mini Cooper, and Volkswagen Beetle already look like characters before you touch them.

Here's a good way to approach trunk-or-treat: picture the car's headlights as the eyes and the grille (or the lack of one on many EVs) as the mouth, and take it from there. This can easily mean a jack-o'-lantern, a ghost with a white sheet over the front of the car, or the IRS man, depending on what scares you the most. The ghost is the easiest of the three: drape a white sheet over the nose, cut eyeholes where the headlights sit, and clip or tape it down so it doesn't flap loose.

Remember, these ideas are for parked cars only, so anything covering your headlights, windows, or license plate needs to come off before you drive anywhere. And you can let your imagination go wild, but be sure to use safe and proven products so you don't cause any damage to your car.

This is the trunk-or-treat classic, and it's a classic for a good reason. The cargo area is already a built-in stage, so all you need is a theme. A graveyard is the easy pick: cut tombstones out of foam board, paint them gray, and prop them up with a plastic skeleton arm reaching out from under the cargo cover.

If you want to see the whole thing come together, this cardboard graveyard built in the back of an SUV by Crafty Chica is also a good place to start. If graveyards feel played out, a witch's lair or a mad scientist's lab works just as well. Think bubbling "potions" in jars and a few props that look like they belong in a haunted garage.

You can also turn the trunk into a gas station, though, with prices at the pump what they are, that's arguably the scariest option on this list. The best part is the handout, so turn the candy into the gimmick. A cardboard coffin that slides out treats or a "feed the monster" bin with a big cartoon mouth will have kids lining up.

title: Switching Auto Insurance Providers: The Pros And Cons Explained
raw_summary: Chances are pretty high that, if you're reading this, you've got auto insurance. Chances are also pretty high that you think you're spending a bit more than you should be on it. You're not alone — insurance premiums have been steadily rising for the past couple of years across the whole country. Higher prices on new cars, more tech, and more expensive repairs all contribute to the problem of rising auto insurance rates. What's a person to do? Well, switching auto insurance providers is one way to get yourself a lower premium, often for identical or nearly identical coverage. When people switch auto insurance it's often because the new company has discounts the old one just doesn't offer, or is running promotions to win over new customers. Sometimes a review of the kinds of coverage you're paying for, and what you're actually using, can reveal places to find savings too. Of course, great rewards frequently have some challenges baked in.

When people switch auto insurance it's often because the new company has discounts the old one just doesn't offer, or is running promotions to win over new customers. Sometimes a review of the kinds of coverage you're paying for, and what you're actually using, can reveal places to find savings too. Of course, great rewards frequently have some challenges baked in.
Switching auto insurance providers can be a quick and easy process, but there are some pros and cons to consider before you make the jump. Let's get into it!

This is the headliner, and it's pretty obvious: you can save money by switching your auto insurance provider! Really, though, you don't have to switch providers to save money — you could reduce the amount of coverage you have, increase your deductible, or skip some of the add-ons like a lower glass deductible or rental car coverage.

Many companies offer new customers deals and discounts to entice them to move from a competitor. Be sure to get quotes not only for auto, but for bundles that the company offers, as some significantly discount their premiums when a customer also purchases renters or homeowners insurance. Some auto insurance companies may also offer lower premiums with programs not offered at your current insurer, like discounts for safe driving when you allow them to monitor your habits with an app or device that attaches to your car.

Yep, there are a few downsides to consider when you are hoping to save money by switching your auto insurance provider. Perhaps the first one to plan for is the fact that you need money to save money.

Zero money down auto insurance isn't a thing, so you'll need a cash up front to start a new policy. If you've already paid your policy in full, your current auto insurer should refund you for the unused portion of your current policy, but it doesn't happen instantly. Depending on your insurer and the processing methods they prefer, you could potentially be waiting a few weeks to get that refund check. That means, unfortunately, you'll need to have some money on hand to make the switch. Think of it like renting a new apartment — you'll need to have a deposit to get moved in.

One way to mitigate this is through monthly payment plans, which could help coordinate a changeover from one insurer to another without having to wait on a refund check. Make sure the new policy is active before you cancel the old one, otherwise you may end up flagged for a lapse in coverage. Still, if your goal is to maximize savings, you can often get a nice discount if you're willing to pay in full. What you're able to do is going to depend on your personal financial situation, so be sure to ask whether the price you're seeing is dependent on a certain payment frequency or having autopay turned on.

raw_title: Why Did Dodge, Ford, And Other Muscle Cars Use Window Louvers?
title: Why Did Dodge, Ford, And Other Muscle Cars Use Window Louvers?
raw_summary: A big V8 making more horsepower than anyone could justify was only part of the package in a 1960s or 1970s muscle car. Detroit's factory hot rods also popularized features like hood scoops, all manner of bold graphics , and a trend for window louvers on performance cars that continued long after the original muscle car craze died. Window louvers are the slats you sometimes see on the back of cars, like the 1969 Ford Mustang Boss 302 or second-generation Chevy Camaros. They're dark-colored horizontal strips of metal or plastic, joined together to form a frame that sits on top of the rear widow. You'll sometimes see them fitted to notchback coupes, cars with a more traditional three-box silhouette. But usually its fastbacks that saw the louver treatment. And there's a good reason for that. A car interior can get really hot when the sun's rays are blasting a large expanse of shallowly raked glass on a fastback muscle car. And that was a problem in the late 1960s when this body style was more popular.

Window louvers are the slats you sometimes see on the back of cars, like the 1969 Ford Mustang Boss 302 or second-generation Chevy Camaros.

They're dark-colored horizontal strips of metal or plastic, joined together to form a frame that sits on top of the rear widow. You'll sometimes see them fitted to notchback coupes, cars with a more traditional three-box silhouette. But usually its fastbacks that saw the louver treatment. And there's a good reason for that. A car interior can get really hot when the sun's rays are blasting a large expanse of shallowly raked glass on a fastback muscle car. And that was a problem in the late 1960s when this body style was more popular.

Air conditioning was still an expensive option back then, and window tints were in their infancy, so drivers looked for new ways to keep cool. And, let's be honest, to look it. Like slatted shutters on a house window, car window louvers help minimize the effect of the sun, without totally blocking out the light. But also like residential shutters, car window louvers improve privacy and have a very distinctive look, one that added to the gritty visual appeal of a muscle car back in the day.

House builders have used louvers for thousands of years, and automakers have stamped metal louvers into panels to vent engine heat since at least Buick Roadmasters from the 1940s. But the best known early automotive use of louvers as we understand them, is on the Lamborghini Miura. The Miura debuted at the 1966 Geneva Auto Show with a plexiglass window covering its 4.0L V12, but Lamborghini's engineers soon realized the screen trapped huge amounts of heat generated by the 350-horsepower engine.

Designer Marcello Gandini replaced the window with louvers, and 60 years on it's hard to imagine the Miura without them. Other automakers soon picked up on the trend. Ford — which had already employed fixed metal louvers on the rear quarter windows for its 1965 Mustang — offered rear window "Sports Slats" on 1969 Mustangs ordered with the SportRoof fastback body. A year later, Chrysler rolled out louver packages on the Dodge Challenger and Plymouth Barracuda. Both types were made from aluminum and fitted over the rear window, rather than replacing it, as the Miura's had.

By the mid-1970s, America's aftermarket industry was offering louver kits for dozens of different models. Japanese coupes like the Datsun 280Z and Mazda RX-7 were prime for a louver makeover, and kits often featured matching rear quarter-light louvers. They were still popular through the 1980s, and although the rise of window tints and the smooth, aerodynamic styling of the 1990s saw louvers fall out of favor, they've since gained a second life. Lamborghini still references the Miura's louvers on its modern Temerario and Reveulto supercars, Chevy deploys them on its ultra-high performance C8 Corvette ZR1 , and you can buy aftermarket louvers for everything from the Toyota GR86 to the BMW 4 Series.
bullet_points: A big V8 making more horsepower than anyone could justify was only part of the package in a 1960s or 1970s muscle car.

Detroit's factory hot rods also popularized features like hood scoops, all manner of bold graphics , and a trend for window louvers on performance cars that continued long after the original muscle car craze died.

Today, this is a company known for reliability, practicality, and the signature symmetrical all-wheel drive that features in almost all its vehicles. These are all attributes that serve an SUV well, and to that end, of the ten Subaru models on sale in the U.S. today, seven of them are SUVs. The Crosstrek is the company's most-popular model, with nearly 200,000 units sold in 2025 alone, though whether anyone believes the Crosstrek is an actual SUV is up for debate — and not just because it is the smallest of the seven.

For enthusiasts in the market for the brand's practical and capable AWD models, here's a rundown of the Japanese automaker's current portfolio of new SUVs sold on the North American market, ranked from smallest to largest according to their total length in inches. Four of these use boxer-four gasoline engines or lightly hybridized versions of the same, while the other three are electric vehicles (EVs) that were born out of a tie-up with Toyota. From the Crosstrek to the Ascent and everything in between, there's serious off-road prowess available in all of these models and even the sort of off-the-line acceleration that can shame sports cars. Perhaps the development team at Subaru remembers the "good old days" after all.

One glance at the Subaru Crosstrek, and you may consider it nothing more than a jacked-up hatchback on chunky tires — especially the base model, which doesn't even get roof rails. However, the Crosstrek is Consumer Reports' "Top Subcompact SUV" in 2026 and, like every Subaru off-roader, it features the company's symmetrical AWD, so in theory, it is at least somewhat equipped for the wilderness. Heck, there's even a Wilderness grade, which can walk the walk while talking the talk.

Starting at $28,415 for the base 2026 model, the Crosstrek gets its power from a 2.5-liter boxer-4 that delivers 180 horsepower and 178 pound-feet of torque in most versions. There's also a hybrid option for the Sport and Limited cars, which raises those numbers to 194 hp and 199 lb-ft, combined. Despite the extra performance, these hybrid Crosstreks are more economical, which might matter more to some buyers than its off-road prowess.

At just 176.4 inches long, the Crosstrek is the most compact SUV Subaru makes, so it'll be easy to park and maneuver in urban areas. And while we perhaps wouldn't take it clambering up the Rubicon, the Crosstrek has 8.7 inches of ground clearance — that's as good as anything else on this list, save for Wilderness versions of the Forester and Outback. Meanwhile, the Crosstrek Wilderness gets more clearance at 9.3 inches, along with better approach and departure angles.

All Crosstrek trims weigh between roughly 3,300 pounds and no more than 3,700 pounds for the hybrids, and while every other version can tow up to 1,500 lbs, the Wilderness manages a massive 3,500 lbs thanks to various upgrades. That sounds like an SUV to us — certainly more so than a Toyota Corolla Cross.

Born from a joint venture with compatriot Toyota, the arguably more appealing Subaru Uncharted represents the entry point to zero-emission Subaru ownership, starting from $36,945 with destination. It is a little longer than the Crosstrek at 177.8 inches long, and its trunk holds a little more cargo, but it offers slightly less ground clearance at 8.2 inches, which speaks volumes about its street-biased nature. In fact, if you want an all-wheel-drive Uncharted, you've got to avoid the Premium FWD. This model has just one motor on the front axle, providing a modest 221 hp and 199 lb-ft of torque. That'll see the Uncharted from 0 to 60 mph in around 6.5 seconds (via Motor Trend ).

title: Why China's GAC Tried Developing A 4-Cylinder Engine That Ran On Ammonia

summary: A few years ago, in 2023, China's Guangzhou Automobile Group Co. (GAC) pioneered a four-cylinder engine that runs on ammonia. In part because ammonia, like hydrogen, can burn without generating carbon emissions, because it's composed of nitrogen and hydrogen (the chemical formula is NH3), so it doesn't contain any carbon atoms to emit.
article_paragraphs: A few years ago, in 2023, China's Guangzhou Automobile Group Co. (GAC) pioneered a four-cylinder engine that runs on ammonia. But why bother? In part because ammonia, like hydrogen, can burn without generating carbon emissions, because it's composed of nitrogen and hydrogen (the chemical formula is NH3), so it doesn't contain any carbon atoms to emit.

GAC said at the time that its two-liter engine would burn liquid ammonia and produce up to 161 hp with a 90% reduction in carbon emissions versus an engine that ran on gasoline. But that explanation should make you scratch your head. Why 90% and not 100%, since we just told you there's no carbon to burn?

Well, in part because ammonia won't stay liquid at non-Arctic temperatures. So you have to cool it to below -28 degrees Fahrenheit, and you also need to keep it under pressure. In turn, when it's cold, it doesn't really want to ignite. Which is probably why GAC's solution was to add some gasoline to the ammonia in order to get it to combust.

As if that's not the only issue, ammonia on its own is only half as energy dense as gasoline. But there are upsides. First, you can make so-called green hydrogen via electrolysis directly from water. This produces hydrogen and oxygen, and ammonia can then be further split off from the hydrogen, ideally with the entire process run via renewable energy, such as solar. Speaking of hydrogen, carmakers like Toyota keep trying to push hydrogen as a viable car fuel, but that's not as energy dense as ammonia and has pretty substantial range challenges. But if you can produce green ammonia, you have a carbon-free fuel without the concerns like slower EV fueling and heavy batteries, right? Yeah... but.

Okay, so ammonia is more energy dense than hydrogen. But it's still only about half as energy dense as gasoline. Which is partly why, yes, you've seen ammonia tech coming faster to shipping than to cars, where that density is less of a challenge. Also, a by-product of ammonia combustion is nitrogen emissions, which cause toxic air that's bad for human breathing. However, at the time GAC presented its findings, the carmaker said it had also tackled the latter issue, which is good news if true.

But there are yet more quandaries. For instance, ammonia likes to corrode metal, and especially galvanized metals, like iron, copper, brass and copper alloys. Every fitting has to be made of steel. That part, perhaps, is something that can be tackled in the engine bay — but there's still the challenge of fueling and transporting the stuff. Imagine trying to keep it liquified for cooling, and keeping it refrigerated in underground storage that you typically have at a gas station, and the hazards that it presents , including nausea, blistering, and all sorts of other fun, according to the CDC . Then again, we do blithely tend to accept liquid petroleum's icks, like the fact that gasoline is a known carcinogen.

Meanwhile, carmakers beyond GAC (which is a partner of Toyota) keep pushing ammonia's boundaries. In fact, Daihatsu, which is a Toyota subsidiary, just released a new ammonia engine concept, and so has Toyota's own division, Toyota Industries. Probably for good reason, they both seem to have arrived at a way to combine using both hydrogen and ammonia together.

We just told you that ammonia has a higher energy density than hydrogen. Also, hydrogen has to be stored at much higher pressure and colder temperatures. But then, ammonia has both a combustion issue, and an emissions one. What if you derived the ammonia from hydrogen, stored that (rather than hydrogen) in the car, then converted it back to hydrogen for power production? That solves a bit of the density problem of hydrogen and the combustion problem of ammonia, and seems to be what's going on with two different engine concepts.

title: XCMG debuts new, fully autonomous electric terminal tractor [video]
raw_summary: The new XCMG SDA411 concept terminal truck is fully electric, has no cabin, and an L4 autonomous tech stack that’s purpose-built for unmanned logistics – and, if XCMG get their way, it looks like the future of drayage truck operations. Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification . It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.

Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification . It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.
Chinese equipment brand XCMG gets it , and they’re taking the electric terminal truck concept a step further with the debut of an all-new, cab-less design that’s 100% autonomous.

“With no cab and an L4 autonomous driving system, the platform is purpose-built for unmanned logistics,” said XCMG, on LinkedIn . “Its 360° perception system enables autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, task execution and parking, supporting continuous mixed-traffic operations in demanding environments.”

That same post included a video showing the SDA411 make its way around XCMG’s campus, making some emergency stops, and pulling up to a charger for a human attendant to plug it in ( I guess they haven’t heard about Fortescue’s trick with the KUKA welding robot , yet). You can check out the post for yourself, below.

As for the autonomous aspect, while I generally side with labor and humanity over management and technology, there’s some truth to the industry claims that young people don’t want to drive trucks anymore, even with the promise of six-figure salaries.

Combine that with an aging workforce and not enough new talent entering the field, and virtually every industrial sector is struggling with a serious operator shortage . Autonomous equipment like the SDA411 could help address that shortage, keeping goods moving even when there aren’t enough drivers to go around. And rather than simply replacing workers, the technology could let experienced operators oversee multiple vehicles, take on supervisory roles and stay in the industry longer, while making these jobs accessible to people who might not otherwise be able to do them .

If XCMG get their way, we’ll get to see how that all plays out somewhat sooner than later. In the meantime, we’ll have to settle for hearing what you think about the SDA411 and how it could impact brands like Kalmar and Orange EV in the comments.

title: Porsche Expands 'Do Not Drive' Recall For Performance Models With Center-Lock Wheels That Could Fall Off
raw_summary: The recalls have really been flowing lately, and not always from the automakers you might expect ( Ahem, Ford .) In truly rare form, Germany's crown jewel Porsche expanded a 2024 recall to include an additional 548 of its highest-performing cars, because their center-lock wheels might fall off. What sounds like a movie plotline to take out some of the wealthy elite is actually an unfortunate supplier defect, as the NHTSA Recall Report states. The latest batch of Porsches involved in this recall include the 2024 911 Turbo (13 cars), 2024 911 S/T (39 cars), 2024 911 GT3 RS (41 cars), 2024 911 GT3 (50 cars), 2024 718 Spyder RS (70 cars), 2024 718 Cayman GT4 RS (73 cars), 2024 911 Turbo S (94 cars), and 2024 911 GTS (168 cars). Porsche says owners of these cars should not drive them until a Porsche dealer has checked the center-lock wheel fastening system and replaced any out-of-specification parts.

The latest batch of Porsches involved in this recall include the 2024 911 Turbo (13 cars), 2024 911 S/T (39 cars), 2024 911 GT3 RS (41 cars), 2024 911 GT3 (50 cars), 2024 718 Spyder RS (70 cars), 2024 718 Cayman GT4 RS (73 cars), 2024 911 Turbo S (94 cars), and 2024 911 GTS (168 cars). Porsche says owners of these cars should not drive them until a Porsche dealer has checked the center-lock wheel fastening system and replaced any out-of-specification parts.

The original recall issued almost exactly three years ago on October 28, 2024, included 1,851 2024 911 Turbos and 718 GT4 RS and Spyder RS models, so now a total of 2,399 cars are affected. 100% of those cars included in the first recall were estimated to be affected by the fault, but just 1.4% of the cars included in the new recall are expected to be affected.

Fortunately, Porsche says immediate vibration should be perceptible if the center lock fractures on anyone's car, so if you're driving a 2024 Porsche sports car that suddenly starts vibrating, you might want to pull over as soon as possible.

Porsche is aware of several incidents attributable to center lock fractures, and the only description of the cause provided says, "analyses of the affected material batch confirmed lead and bismuth contents outside the specification." The only other mentions of the issue say "...the center wheel lock components used in the center wheel fastening system within certain production ranges were manufactured out of specification."

The latest do-not-drive warning arose after two additional field accidents involving fractured center lock components earlier this year in May and August, though no injuries were reported. Owners needn't worry about reimbursement for the repairs, since all affected cars are still covered under their warranty. Owners will be contacted by phone, email, and MyPorsche App push notifications by December 15, though VINs are already searchable on NHTSA's website.

raw_title: New Li Auto i6 Goes 811 km (504 Miles)
title: New Li Auto i6 Goes 811 km (504 Miles)
raw_summary: Li Auto’s new i6 electric vehicle has a very interesting look. It makes me think of something out of some futuristic movie or The Jetsons . It certainly has an MPV (multipurpose vehicle) design that is current in China but not really anywhere else. Anyway, aside from the futuristic, cool styling, the new i6 has great specs and features. The i6 has a CLTC-rated range of 780 km (485 miles), but the company recently livestreamed a drive in which the vehicle drove 811 km (504 miles) before reaching 0%. This was using 11.8 kWh/100 km. The vehicle has a 96 kWh battery.

It certainly has an MPV (multipurpose vehicle) design that is current in China but not really anywhere else. Anyway, aside from the futuristic, cool styling, the new i6 has great specs and features.

It certainly has an MPV (multipurpose vehicle) design that is current in China but not really anywhere else. Anyway, aside from the futuristic, cool styling, the new i6 has great specs and features.

The i6 has a CLTC-rated range of 780 km (485 miles), but the company recently livestreamed a drive in which the vehicle drove 811 km (504 miles) before reaching 0%. This was using 11.8 kWh/100 km. The vehicle has a 96 kWh battery.

Interestingly, Li Auto has shifted away from using CATL batteries. It is using in-house batteries that CALB and Sunwoda helped to manufacture. “ Dian Dong Che Zhu Ren , a Chinese automotive outlet, reports that this design change allows the i6 to carry an extra 3 kWh of cells. It also claims that Li Auto’s latest SiC power modules feature revised current paths that reduce operational losses and add 30 km of winter driving range,” CarNewsChina writes.

“The 5C charging-capable Lian Shan battery is likely to roll out to Li Auto’s existing lineup, and the automaker is also betting big on its safety capabilities. It pledges that Lian Shan packs will never self-ignite or combust in collisions, and like Xiaomi’s Dragonscale batteries, Li Auto is offering up a free new car if they do.”

As far as the endurance test goes, it was not one of those hardcore hypermiler attempts. It included realistic use of the car. “Li Auto says it conducted the test around Lake Tai ( Taihu) in the Yangtze Delta, with temperatures between 13 and 20°C. The i6 carried four occupants, their luggage, and 50 kg of additional gear. The automaker stresses that the air conditioning was on during the 18-hour drive,” CarNewsChina adds. The drive occurred in city driving conditions with speed limits between 40 and 80 km/h. So, yes, the car went much further than it would have on the highway driving much faster. Also note that the car didn’t die when it got to 0%. They just stopped the test then, without pushing to see how far the battery buffer from 0% down to dead would take them.

Refrigerated trailers (reefers) are critical for hauling fresh food and flowers from the farm to your local market — the problem is that they pollute like crazy, powered by high sulfur, red-dye diesel-powered generators that run around the clock, even if the truck pulling them is fully electric. That constant diesel burn spews CO₂ and NOx into industrial and residential areas alike , and contributes significantly to fleets’ carbon emissions and noise pollution at a time when a number of municipalities are moving to regulate both.

It is, as they say, “a real problem,” but Sunswap Endurance cracked it with a solar-powered reefer that can keep food and pharmaceuticals cold in transit without burning a drop of diesel fuel – and now, they have real customers.

One of Australia’s largest privately owned trucking companies, Wickham Freight Lines decided to purchase the Sunswap Endurance solar trailer units following an initial trial, running from Sydney to Brisbane and back this past summer on a route covering a total of 1,670 km (~1,040 miles) over more than 30 hours of driving.
After Wickham’s drivers finished the round trip with over 65% of the battery’s capacity still left, the purchase was a no-brainer.

“I put the Sunswap Endurance into the fleet and told the team to stretch it — treat it as a normal unit,” explains Graham Keogh, director at Wickham Freight Lines . “We were genuinely impressed. I’m a true believer. I love the technology and I’m not a true tech person whatsoever. You can just see that it’s a winner … the performance, reliability and operational savings were beyond what we expected. For a business like ours, running a large fleet across the east coast, with a heavy focus on refrigerated and cold chain freight, this technology makes real commercial sense.”

Sunswap Endurance first showed their new solar reefer unit at HVIA TruckShowX in Hunter Valley this May past. It’s compelling, insultingly simple technology and I, for one, hope this customer delivery is just the first of many. Let us know what you think of these guys, in the comments.

article_paragraphs: It took two weeks to shoot the 12 most famous minutes of the 1968 film "Bullitt." Sounds like overkill, but the scene is just one of the ways Hollywood icon Steve McQueen became inexorably connected with high-speed shenanigans on- and off-screen. Love it or hate it, no list of racing films is complete without mention of the 1971 flick "Le Mans." McQueen's love for racing extended beyond the movies, and he famously took to the track under the alias Harvey Mushman. Seriously, you can't make this stuff up.

The King of Cool, as he was also known, could be a bit mercurial, as it turns out. Enough so that he repeatedly lost his cool on set, ticked off a couple of other leading movie men in the process, and made something of a reputation for himself. Two of these leading actors included fellow car guys and racing drivers James Garner and Paul Newman.

Things got heated enough between McQueen and Garner that the latter wasn't shy about calling the former out after working together on the set of "The Great Escape." Newman wasn't so keen on McQueen, either. We'll explore these disagreements below, which still prompt movie and motorsport fans to compare the racing careers and accolades of all three Hollywood leading men, from Sebring to Le Mans.

Big actors have to spend their time (and money) off-screen doing something, right? In the case of Steve McQueen, Paul Newman, and James Garner, cars and motorsport were irresistible. McQueen managed to place second alongside Peter Revson at the 12 Hours of Sebring, coming in just behind the last American international racing legend himself, Mario Andretti. Newman's racing career spanned 35 years and a dozen championships as a driver and team owner. Garner was an Off-Road Motorsports Hall of Fame inductee who raced in everything from the Indianapolis 500 to the NORRA Mexican 1000.

You might think that would be enough to squash any set beef and keep things civil among petrolheads. Not so much. While Newman and McQueen were co-stars in the 1974 movie, "The Towering Inferno," the two reportedly hit a boiling point. Newman called the Bullitt star a "chickens**t" following McQueen's rage over Newman having 12 more lines than him. The two then feuded over billing on the film's posters and credits until the studio settled on double top billing.

Garner, even with his good guy repute in show business, had some choice words for McQueen, labeling the actor a "poser who cultivated the image of a macho man" after working with him on the set of "The Great Escape." Ouch. McQueen's behavior on "The Great Escape" also prompted Garner to say, "Steve could be a stubborn little cuss, but the director added some motorcycle stunts to pacify him and changed his character to a guy who goes out to reconnoiter the countryside then unselfishly allows himself to be recaptured so he can share information with others."

A love for all things fast, fun, and dangerous wasn't enough to keep McQueen from a strained relationship with Newman and Garner. If anything, the connection invited competition and frequent comparison. When it came to "The Towering Inferno" co-stars, famed racing driver Dick Barbour applauded both actors, but seemed to give the edge to McQueen for his talent. "Paul was a very methodical driver. He wasn't a natural like Steve. McQueen picked it up immediately," Barbour said . That's coming from a driver who spent time co-driving with Newman and coaching McQueen.

Granted, Garner and McQueen weren't co-stars on the track, but that didn't stop the former from impressing racing royalty. Bob Bondurant, the former Formula 1 racing driver and racing school founder, applauded Garner's skills in the 2006 documentary "Pushing the Limit: The Making of Grand Prix."
