article_paragraphs: America loves trucks. Whether it's a horse trailer or a 30-foot camper, somebody somewhere in the U.S. is hooking it to a pickup right now. On the surface, a full-size truck and a big SUV look cut from the same cloth: both are built for utility, both sit high, and both can pull a trailer. So why are pickups still chosen for big towing jobs?

The short answer: pickups are designed to tow more, and the proof shows up even when a truck and an SUV share the same bones. J.D. Power notes the Chevrolet Tahoe is "built on the same platform as the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 pickup," yet the 2026 Tahoe tops out at 8,400 pounds while the Silverado 1500 is rated for 13,300 pounds. Ford's lineup tells the same story, with the 2026 Expedition maxing out at 9,600 pounds and the 2026 F-150 at 13,500 pounds. SUVs can tow, but they reach their limits sooner, and Consumer Reports warns against towing "at or near your vehicle's capacity."

In heavy-duty territory, the gap becomes a canyon. With Ford's High-Capacity Gooseneck Tow Package, a 2026 F-450 is rated to pull 40,000 pounds, a figure even new SUVs with impressive towing capacities can't come close to. (The Jeep Grand Wagoneer leads the full-size SUV class at 10,000 pounds, which still leaves it behind most full-size pickups.)

Truck beds almost never connect to the cab — the two sit on a heavy frame as separate pieces, since a one-piece body would be too stiff to take the twisting that comes with heavy towing. Most SUVs skip that setup. Take Ford's Explorer, a unibody midsize three-row SUV: it's rated to tow 5,000 pounds, less than half of what an F-150 can pull.

Out back, the classic utilitarian pickup recipe calls for leaf springs. It's old-school hardware, and it's stuck around on trucks because it's the better fit for heavy towing. The trade-off is comfort. Most SUVs ride on coil springs, which give passengers a softer ride but aren't usually set up for big towing jobs. Then there's where the weight sits. As The RV Geeks explain, "a truck can carry more weight positioned right above its rear axle," which is where gooseneck and fifth-wheel hitches go.

Ford's Super Duty ratings show the payoff, with the max rating dropping by 10,000 pounds when you swap a gooseneck for a conventional hitch. Trucks tend to offer more specialized towing equipment such as towing mirrors, trailer brake controllers, specialized axle ratios, and heavy-duty cooling systems. They also tend to have a longer wheelbase compared to a comparably sized SUV – this can be a problem in tight parking spots and crowded city streets, but it helps with stability while towing.

Lastly, there's the engine. Heavy-duty trucks offer big diesels, and the Super Duty's top option makes up to 1,200 lb-ft of torque — not something you can get in an SUV. Put it all together and a pickup isn't just stronger on paper; it's built around the trailer from the frame up.

In terms of people-hauling, six is the ceiling for a full-size pickup. Big SUVs play a different game. The 2026 Chevy Suburban seats up to nine, and third-row riders get 36.7 inches of legroom. Try fitting a carpool into a crew cab. No pickup offers a third row, so the soccer team is out of luck. Size down to the Honda Pilot, and you can still get up to eight seats.

Yet again in 2026, Ferrari falters when it actually counts. That clean sweep of fastest practice times looked so convincing, and yet given it's this team, there was still that element of doubt. Would Ferrari and/or its drivers somehow fumble qualifying? Would something go tactically wrong?
In the end, it just wasn't quick enough in qualifying trim - rivals able to exploit deployment possibilities much better, and Charles Leclerc ruing poor tyre prep too.
And this doesn't seem like a case where qualifying will be the blip and there's loads of untapped race pace in store for Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton to charge forward with.
This Ferrari might just be better at looking quick in the sessions that don't actually matter. - Matt Beer

In the weeks where his coronation as a remarkably young F1 world champion has looked ever more secure, Antonelli has actually been keeping a relatively low profile on track, unable to work his usual magic amid the confusion around Mercedes' upgrade.
So despite the fact he's on the cusp of sealing the title with multiple (who really knows how many) races to spare, Antonelli's pole here feels slightly out of the blue.

raw_title: Public Beaches In Texas Are Also Highways, And You Can Actually Drive On Them
title: Public Beaches In Texas Are Also Highways, And You Can Actually Drive On Them
raw_summary: There's something special about driving down a beach; the slight squeak of sand under your tires, the murmur of the crashing waves, the feel of your vehicle working just a little bit harder, all make you feel like part of the beautiful wild scenery. The early sand racers of Daytona knew the feeling. The 1960's dune buggy culture of Southern California made driving on beaches even cooler. In Texas, drivers embrace beaches in a big way, enjoying over 200 miles of drivable beaches. Texans so enjoy their access to beaches that they coded public access into state law in 1959 with the Open Beaches Act. In 2009, Texans voted with a 76.9% approval rate to add it to the state constitution. Essentially, the area from the low tide line to the line of continuous vegetation is public domain that can not be impeded. The Texas General Land Office is charged with enforcing the Act, and local jurisdictions have some say on what "public access" means to them. There are stipulations such as public safety needs or environmental concerns, for example, which allows a municipality to restrict driving on beaches.

Despite some restrictions, there are a lot of beaches to choose from . Every beach is considered a Texas State Highway, so all traffic laws apply – yes including seatbelts. Flip flops and bare feet are legally allowed. Also, like some highways, you may have to pay to play, as a majority of the beaches have some sort of access fee. Surfside Beach is on the pricey side at $15 daily, while that $15 will get you a year of access and maybe a hot dog or two at Matagorda Beach. Make delicious choices.

There are a handful of free beaches as well. For those into SpaceX, Boca Chica Beach may be the spot for you. Closer to Galveston, the West End beaches offer free access to beaches. The vibe of the beaches varies wildly. Beaches closer to bigger cities can seem like little more than sandy parking lots, but with a little bit of work you can find more solitude.For true privacy, Texas has the "Longest Undeveloped Beach Drive in the World." The Padre Island National Seashore offers 66 miles of beach adventure. This is a wild beach with soft sand and other obstacles, so a four-wheel-drive vehicle is your best bet. There are no services, so come prepared with food, beverages, gas and probably recovery gear. For your efforts, you'll be rewarded with beautiful scenery, plenty of wildlife and a good bit of peace and quiet. Bring a tent and fishing pole and make a couple days out of it!

If you're sold on beach driving, but not actively in Texas, don't fret big fella. There are plenty of places nationwide to get your fix. We mentioned California's dune buggy culture earlier. The "birthplace" of that culture, Oceano Dunes State Vehicular Recreation Area in Southern California just reopened for your driving pleasure. Further north on the west coast, Washington has a 28-mile run out on Long Beach Peninsula. On the east coast, "heading down the Cape" of Cape Cod is a popular summer pastime . Further south, Cape Hatteras National Seashore has over 50 miles of accessible beach, including Corolla Beach, which has wild horses just wandering around, being wild. Go eve further south to Florida and there is, of course, Daytona Beach. Nearby, venture to lesser known New Smyrna Beach, where this writer cut his teeth driving the beach in a beat up old Chevette.

article_paragraphs: Born in Germany in the late 1870s, the Duesenberg brothers — Frederick (Fred) and August (Augie) – would move to America and make some of the time's most luxurious and innovative cars. One of their earliest ventures included opening a garage in Iowa circa 1903 – which is where they landed after immigrating. During this time, Fred and August were modifying and racing cars.

Now, we're skipping a lot of steps here, but after gaining a reputation as brilliant engineers — and developing motors for the military during World War I – the brothers found themselves in New Jersey. The Garden State proved to be fertile soil for the two, as that's where the first Duesenberg straight-8 engine was created.

Straight-8 power became a defining characteristic of Duesenberg race cars, which in turn became some of the era's most dominant performers. They not only won at Indy — claiming the checkered flag three times during the 1920s — but also at Le Mans.

Le Mans was where Jimmy Murphy ran away from the field, winning by about 14 minutes over heavily favored early motorsports pioneer Ralph DePalma. Just keep in mind we're talking about the 1921 French Grand Prix here, not the 24-hour endurance race used by the likes of Michelin to refine its tire designs .

A key Le Mans advantage for the Duesenbergs was that their latest cars now sported four-wheel hydraulic brakes. Fred would file patents for his four-wheel hydraulic-brake setup in 1920, with the system being deployed for the brothers' first passenger car a year later. This development made the 1921 Duesenberg Model A the first production car with that particular technology.

While the Duesenberg Model A was the first production-series vehicle with four-wheel hydraulic brakes, the brothers couldn't claim they invented the technology. Let's take a closer look at what preceded the Model A's brakes and how these events influenced the system's design.

The first solid evidence of four-wheel mechanical brakes comes with the 1912 Argyll 15 HP, with a system developed by Henri Perrot. The French engineer would earn the first U.S. patent for a four-wheel mechanical brake system in 1913 while working for Argyll.

Next, sources credit a company called Knox Motors with offering a form of hydraulic brakes on the rear wheels of its commercial trucks as early as 1915. Little known today, Knox also built one of the world's first motorized fire trucks.

article_paragraphs: MotoGP championship contender Jorge Martin may be targeting a sooner than expected return to race action after the Phillip Island injury that seemed to have ended his title shot.
Martin’s Aprilia team announced on Sunday morning that Martin will remain in Australia this week despite breaking his arm on Saturday during the sprint race.
That potentially opens the door for an attempted return at Sepang in one week’s time.

Initial reports from the team on Saturday afternoon suggested that Martin had broken both the radius and ulna in his right arm, but said that he would first travel to hospital in Melbourne (two hours away from the Phillip Island track) for further assessment.
That assessment turned out to be good news, with a suspected fracture of his ulna (the smaller bone in the lower arm) ruled out.
“Jorge Martin underwent a CT scan to assess his condition following yesterday’s injury. The only confirmed injury is a non-displaced fracture of the distal radius,” said Aprilia’s statement.
“Consequently, the rider will not be returning to Spain and will undergo the necessary treatment over the coming days.”

With MotoGP travelling directly from Australia to Malaysia for the next of its back-to-back races at Sepang, the news that Martin will not go back home but will instead remain in the region very much opens the door for an attempt to return next weekend.

article_paragraphs: Volkswagen is offering its Chinese-market Jetta M6 electric sedan with nearly 290 miles of CLTC-rated range for less than $12,000 (USD), and if that’s not what “der people’s wagen” should be all about, I don’t know what is.

Launched as a joint venture between FAW and Volkswagen Group, the Jetta brand’s first battery electric car is finally here – and it is a genuinely accessible , capable , and kinda decent-looking family sedan in the same way VW’s original Type I was when it was first developed in the 1940s.

The new Jetta M6 was launched earlier this in three variants: the 465 Pro, 555 Max and 555 Ultra; each priced at 79,800 yuan (~$11,800), 89,800 yuan and 99,800 yuan, respectively, with the model numbers corresponding to the car’s estimated CLTC range in kilometers (which maths out around ~285 and 345 miles, if you’re curious).

Built on FAW’s Jiesi architecture , the M6 measures 4,806 mm long and 1,868 mm wide, putting it right in that sedan sweet spot between the Civic/Corolla and Accord/Camry crews, and within a few mm this way and that of the Tesla Model 3, so it should have plenty of room for young professionals and families – but the M6′ real selling point is its tech.

Inside, the Jetta M6 offers an 8.88″ driver display along with a big 15.6″ central touchscreen that integrates Chinese AI assistants Doubao and DeepSeek and ships with Apple CarPlay baked in. Advanced ADAS with , “intelligent cruise assistance, automatic emergency braking, and automated parking” is standard.

The entry-level “465 Pro” version of the Jetta M6 comes equipped with 42.9 kWh LFP battery and a 113 kW (~150 hp) electric motor driving the front wheels, a combination the company says is good for a 8.3-second sprint to 100 km/h (62 mph). Stepping up to the 555 versions gets you a larger 51.9 kWh battery and more powerful 145 kW (~195 hp) motor that cuts that sprint to 6.8 seconds.
Both the 42.9 and 51.0 kWh batteries are lithium iron phosphate deals supplied by CALB, with charging from 20% to 80% taking about 30 minutes.

Would those features and performance numbers be enough to get you to look at something like this in the US, even at twice the price? It seems to me that North America’s VW dealers need all the help they can get, and a volume leader like this with a “back to basics” ad campaign that plays on a different kind of nostalgia – nostalgia for a time when people could afford a Jetta , maybe? – could be a winner. Let us know what you think in the comments.

title: Antonelli on US GP pole as Ferrari challenge falls apart
raw_summary: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix as practice pacesetter Ferrari watched its challenge crumble in qualifying. Antonelli came good as the qualifying hour went on and beat Verstappen by 0.179s in Q3 to clinch his seventh pole position of the season, while Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three.
summary: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix as practice pacesetter Ferrari watched its challenge crumble in qualifying. Antonelli came good as the qualifying hour went on and beat Verstappen by 0.179s in Q3 to clinch his seventh pole position of the season, while Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three.
article_paragraphs: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix as practice pacesetter Ferrari watched its challenge crumble in qualifying.
Antonelli came good as the qualifying hour went on and beat Verstappen by 0.179s in Q3 to clinch his seventh pole position of the season, while Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three.

Antonelli was one of three drivers - alongside Mercedes team-mate George Russell and the McLaren of Oscar Piastri - to go through Q1 on mediums in order to save an extra set of soft tyres for Q3. (Something Red Bull did too by running Verstappen and Hadjar on one set of softs in Q1 and Q2.)
Having been sixth in Q1, Antonelli then ended Q2 just 0.080s off the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc at the top of the Q2 order, and jumped to provisional pole at the start of Q3 with a 1m34.035s.

He had been more than a tenth up on that time through the second sector on his final attempt, but then had a big correction on the exit of the Turn 13 right-hander that wrecked that attempt and appeared to open the door to his rivals.

But the Red Bulls failed to improve their times - both actually had their final, slower efforts scrubbed off for track-limits offences - and with Leclerc finding less than a tenth, that meant Antonelli held on to pole.
Verstappen said in failing to beat Antonelli that, having come through Q1 and Q2 on the same set of tyres, "for whatever reason on both of those sets [in Q3] I didn't have a good balance".
Third for Hadjar marked a drastic turnaround for the second Red Bull driver after struggling throughout practice, as Ferrari's fortunes went the other way.

raw_title: 6 WD-40 Myths Gearheads Need To Stop Believing
title: 6 WD-40 Myths Gearheads Need To Stop Believing
raw_summary: If someone came to you selling a product with an incredible range of uses made from a secret formula first tested on missiles, you might think it's BS. However, this progression represents WD-40's actual origin. WD-40 was created by the Rocket Chemical Company, which was founded in 1953 by Norm Larsen. Three Rocket Chemical staff members achieved the product's formula after 40 trials, which is naturally where the name WD-40 comes from. What goes into the formula is considered a trade secret, like the recipe for Coca-Cola, Kentucky Fried Chicken, or the Tesla FSD data snagged by Dutch regulators . Furthermore, trade secrets don't expire the way patents do. Aerospace contractor Convair initially used WD-40 on its Atlas Missile (America's first successful intercontinental ballistic missile) to protect against rust and corrosion.

article_paragraphs: If someone came to you selling a product with an incredible range of uses made from a secret formula first tested on missiles, you might think it's BS. However, this progression represents WD-40's actual origin.

WD-40 was created by the Rocket Chemical Company, which was founded in 1953 by Norm Larsen. Three Rocket Chemical staff members achieved the product's formula after 40 trials, which is naturally where the name WD-40 comes from. What goes into the formula is considered a trade secret, like the recipe for Coca-Cola, Kentucky Fried Chicken, or the Tesla FSD data snagged by Dutch regulators . Furthermore, trade secrets don't expire the way patents do. Aerospace contractor Convair initially used WD-40 on its Atlas Missile (America's first successful intercontinental ballistic missile) to protect against rust and corrosion.
When discussing WD-40, it's important to recognize the range of stories that aren't true. Below are six WD-40 myths that continue circulating, some of which are downright baffling.

If you've been reading Jalopnik recently, you'll know this one isn't true. Right off the bat, you shouldn't use it on your wiper blades ; it's terrible for squeaky engine belts , and it can lead to some entertaining damage if you replace your engine oil with the stuff .

Part of the misconception has to do with WD-40's lubricating properties. The company itself says that the Multi-Use Product is "a unique, special blend of lubricants" that works to keep your car's door hinges and hood latches moving free and easy. It's just that the experts don't always agree. Yes, WD-40 may help in the short term, but it will quickly evaporate and, in some cases, clean off and dry up the original factory grease.

On the other hand, WD-40 is still too slippery to spray on your brake components, and that's no matter how squeaky they sound. Moreover, that noise could be telling you it's time for new brakes, anyway.

Just remember that we're talking about WD-40's traditional Multi-Use Product here. The company has a full family of WD-40 products that can pick up the slack where the regular stuff isn't up for the job. To properly lubricate parts long-term, like those door hinges, for instance, the company makes WD-40 White Lithium Grease.
Since WD-40 has some lubricating properties, some might think it could do the same for your joints. While many know it cannot, we'll still explore where this ridiculous misconception can stem from.

title: Canada And EU Are Slip Sliding Away On Vehicle Emissions
raw_summary: J. Wellington Wimpy, of Popeye comics fame, had a favorite expression. It went like this: “I will gladly pay you Tuesday for a cheeseburger today.” As the Earth gets hotter and hotter, most countries have made commitments to reduce their climate warming emissions by 2030, or 2050, or 2077, or 2100. Their position papers and high level speeches are filled with passionate promises and flowery language, but their actions seldom match their pious protestations. This week, Canada and the EU both backed away from their existing commitments to reduce motor vehicle emissions. Oh, they still promise to get around to it, just not now, while political turmoil is roiling their economies. The promises will be kept — make no mistake about that — just not now. They need breathing room to attend to the high prices resulting from America’s failed effort to wipe Iran off the map and to address extreme right wing movements who threaten to bring down their governments. There are always plenty of reasons to delay, delay, and delay some more.

This week, Canada and the EU both backed away from their existing commitments to reduce motor vehicle emissions. Oh, they still promise to get around to it, just not now, while political turmoil is roiling their economies. The promises will be kept — make no mistake about that — just not now. They need breathing room to attend to the high prices resulting from America’s failed effort to wipe Iran off the map and to address extreme right wing movements who threaten to bring down their governments. There are always plenty of reasons to delay, delay, and delay some more.

According to Canadian website Electric Autonomy , the government of Canada this week announced a freeze on its vehicle emissions mandates for three years, while promising to still reach its goal of 75 percent of new car sales to be electric by 2035. That and three loonies will get you a doughnut at Tim Horton’s.

The current standard is 172 grams of greenhouse gas emissions per mile (107 grams/km) and it will remain at the level now through the end of 2029. Thereafter, God willing and the creek don’t rise, the standard will begin ratcheting down every year until it reaches 74 grams per mile (46 grams/km).

A joint release by prime minister Mark Carney and Ontario premier Doug Ford said, “Maintaining the fleet average performance standard will provide manufacturers with near-term flexibility at a time when the industry is facing trade-related pressures. It will also provide the ability to generate greenhouse gas credits for use in later years, while continuing to improve emissions performance and fuel economy over time.” In addition to the revised emissions timeline, the federal and Ontario governments are investing $2.5 billion over two years to support capital projects by Canadian auto manufacturers.

Reaction to the new policy has been mixed. Climate activists are disappointed to see any retreat from the emissions standards that were in place, since the new rules will undermine the transition to electric cars. Industries hoped the announcement would bring a sense of direction, clarity, and certainty to the future. In any event, Chinese manufacturers are waiting in the wings, as Canada has opened a door for up to 49,000 Chinese EVs to be imported with only a 6.1 percent tariff.

“[T]he decision to pause any increase in the regulation until model year 2030 puts significantly more pressure on the policy’s later years and could undermine success down the road,” Clean Energy Canada said in a statement. “The unexpected delay will impact the potential benefits of stronger EV uptake, including thousands in fuel cost savings for households and up to $21 billion in charging industry investments. At the same time, Canadian communities will face the increased health costs and impacts from worse air quality.”

Pembina Institute , a British Columbia based clean energy advocacy group, took issue with the new policy, claiming it will make it virtually impossible for Canada to achieve its EV goals. “Earlier this year, the federal government promised stronger vehicle pollution standards starting in 2027, but they are now delaying that to 2029. This makes its goal of 75 per cent EVs by 2035 next to impossible, delaying progress toward giving Canadians more affordable vehicle choices.”

title: New Bentley Supersports Convertible Will Carry On A Silly Yet Awesome Legacy
raw_summary: I think that one of the coolest cars of the 2000s is the first-generation Bentley Continental Supersports. The British automaker took its big GT coupe and made it as rowdy as possible, packing in some surprising lightweighting measures and incredible Piëch-era engineering changes. There was an Supersports version of the second-generation Continental as well, and both models were offered in convertible guise, a silly and incongruous but fully awesome proposition. Bentley removed the rear seats for the Supersports coupes, but the convertibles kept in the small back seat — especially fun on the first-gen car, which was available with the carbon-fiber bucket seats from the Bugatti Veyron up front. Going for the convertible lessened the Supersports' weight savings (and was a bit less sporty in general due to the nature of droptops), and it took a certain kind of buyer to find it appealing.

Bentley removed the rear seats for the Supersports coupes, but the convertibles kept in the small back seat — especially fun on the first-gen car, which was available with the carbon-fiber bucket seats from the Bugatti Veyron up front. Going for the convertible lessened the Supersports' weight savings (and was a bit less sporty in general due to the nature of droptops), and it took a certain kind of buyer to find it appealing.

Now we know Bentley will be continuing on this ridiculous and amazing tradition with the new Supersports , and it'll be the wildest one yet. The fourth-generation Supersports coupe is Bentley's lightest car in 85 years and the first rear-wheel-drive Conti since the '90s, and by far its sportiest offering ever. If you want a big luxurious convertible that's also dynamically inclined and exciting to drive, the new Bentley Supersports convertible will be your only real option.

There's not really a lot to say here. It looks like a convertible version of the Supersports. It's got the same wild carbon-fiber bodykit and prominent rear spoiler, which actually have aerodynamic and performance benefits. We can see the quad exhaust tips that will make a great noise, and a boring Y-spoke wheel design. Sadly the new Supersports doesn't have Bugatti seats, but its carbon-backed front seats are quite nice, and present on this prototype; though the area is all covered up, there's definitely a pair of back seats there, too.

The Supersports coupe is more than 300 pounds lighter than the old V8-powered Continental GT and around 1,100 pounds lighter than a current plug-in-hybrid Conti GT , and those figures will probably hold pretty close for the convertible. That means the droptop Supersports should come in around 4,700 pounds, or about 1,400 pounds heavier than the Porsche 911 GT3 S/C , the kinda-closest equivalent to it. Bentley is only making 500 of the Supersports coupe and they all sold out within a couple months of the car being shown, so I bet the convertible will match that number.

title: 9 Classic Plymouth Models And What They're Worth Today
raw_summary: Hopefully you haven't been in a coma for the last 25 years, because you'd be shocked to know that the once-great Plymouth has been dead since the turn of the century. article_paragraphs: Hopefully you haven't been in a coma for the last 25 years, because you'd be shocked to know that the once-great Plymouth has been dead since the turn of the century. In the 1990s, the vast majority of Plymouth's lineup consisted of badge-engineered versions of various Japanese cars or leftover Dodge products, and it was still only able to muster up about half of Dodge's sales. At the very end, the retro-modern-styled Prowler was the brand's only true Plymouth-designed model.

When it was finally put on the chopping block in 1999, Plymouth was simply not a part of Chrysler's future plans. Done and dusted. But nobody really cares that Plymouth went out at a low point — it's not like we judge Michael Jordan's career based on his final seasons with the Washington Wizards, right? Right.

Plymouth, despite its quiet and underwhelming demise, was a pillar of the American auto industry and delivered some of the most timeless Mopars of the 20th century, some of which you may be interested in for yourself. If that's the case (or if you're simply curious about values), we've conjured up a mix of desirable and important Plymouths, each with an up-to-date estimated value from Hagerty for you to compare against your bank account... and your better judgment.

In contrast to the bleak 1990s version of Plymouth, mid-1950s Plymouth was convincingly in the fight for industry-leading sales figures. It was one of the top three brands in the U.S. by sales in the early part of this decade, but its hold was slipping, and the Plymouth Fury nameplate was one small part of the plan to get this train back on track. The Fury first arrived in 1956 as the high-performance trim of Plymouth's full-size Belvedere. For three model years, the Fury name continued as a mere option (these "sub-series" Belvedere Fury models are actually quite rare), but in 1959, the Fury was spun off as a standalone model.

But now, the Fury itself needed a high-performance trim; hence, the Sport Fury. It only came in two-door configurations, with a hardtop and a slightly more expensive convertible option for those in sunny climates. And because it was the king-of-the-hill version of the Fury, the Sport Fury ditched the typical 230-horsepower two-barrel-carbureted 318 V8 and opted for the four-barrel, 260-horsepower version of the 318 V8 as the standard engine option. There was even an optional 361-cubic-inch "Golden Commando" V8, which boosted the Sport Fury's output to 305 horsepower.

Aside from the motors, the 1959 Sport Fury was a slick piece of machinery at the time, featuring an air-powered leveling system for the rear suspension, swiveling seats (safety first, of course), and an automatically dimming rear-view mirror, among others. In 1959, a Sport Fury cost just under $3,000 (around $30,000 in today's money). Coincidentally, for a good-condition Sport Fury equipped with its standard 318 V8, the estimated value today comes out to around $30,000.

The Plymouth GTX, also known as " the gentleman's muscle car ," appeared right in the midst of the whirlwind of Mopar muscle competition in the mid-to-late 1960s. There was the Satellite, Barracuda, Charger, and eventually the Road Runner, Duster, and Challenger, all vying for the hearts and wallets of those partial to a bit of straight-line speed. And because this came before the Road Runner, the GTX was Plymouth's first real attempt at making a hot Belvedere-based muscle car.

But the GTX isn't just special because it was one of Plymouth's very first attempts at a high-performance automobile. Rather, it's because the GTX never settled for dipping a mere toe into the horsepower wars — it dove straight in. Like LeBron James going directly from high school to the NBA, the GTX's standard engine was the 375-horsepower "Super Commando" 440-cubic-inch V8. Additionally, the only optional engine aside from the standard 440 was the venerable 426 Hemi — quite a brochure, no?

article_paragraphs: Even though Subaru is a Japanese company, many models are built in the United States

Subaru is one of Japan's automotive juggernauts. Established in 1953, it revealed its first model, the 1500, the following year and launched the mass-market 360 in 1958. The company is as Japanese as origami and cherry blossoms, but that doesn't mean it only builds cars in Japan. In fact, Subaru also manufactures vehicles right here in the United States.

Car companies often build vehicles in several countries. For example, Toyota has factories in Japan, Thailand, India, the U.S., Canada, Mexico, France, Poland, and Brazil, among others. Subaru's reach doesn't extend as far, as it builds cars only in its home country and the U.S.

Subaru arrived in the U.S. in 1968, and the popularity of its models surged in the 1970s. As sales rose, Subaru realized it'd be wise to start building cars locally and opened the Subaru of Indiana Automotive (SIA) plant in 1989. More than six million cars have been built at this site, and if you drive a Subaru in the U.S., there's a good chance it was built locally.

The largest model Subaru builds in the U.S. is the Ascent. The three-row SUV comes in seven- and eight-seat configurations and is built exclusively at the Lafayette plant. Subaru launched the Ascent as a successor to the Tribeca in 2018, and while it's now almost a decade old , it still remains surprisingly popular. In fact, sales through the first nine months of this year were up 3.9% from 2025, with 32,556 sold.

Subaru's Indiana plant also produces the Crosstrek . This has long been one of the company's best-selling products in the U.S. and is now in its third generation. From January to September this year, Subaru sold 142,725 units, making it the brand's second best-selling model behind the Forester.

Speaking of the Forester, it is also made in the U.S. Production of the new hybrid Forester kicked off at the Indiana plant in February, while the gas-powered model has been built locally for the past year. Subaru hasn't historically built the Forester in the U.S., as all previous generations were made in Japan. Subaru only recently started local production of it to fill the void left behind by the Outback, which had been built in the U.S. but has now shifted back to Japan. Subaru also built the Legacy in the U.S., but local production ended last September.

title: If Tesla’s Robotaxi Miles Keep Compounding at 20% a Week, the Math Gets Interesting Fast
raw_summary: Tesla just passed Waymo in Austin in weekly driverless miles. If its recent 20% weekly growth holds, it passes Waymo nationally in roughly 11 weeks and is doing the volume of Uber + Lyft across three Texas metros by mid-February. The accumulating unsupervised miles are already large enough to start answering the safety question versus humans and versus Waymo. That has implications for whether LiDAR is actually required.

I noted in my Q3 earnings summary that Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxi miles jumped from 250,000 last quarter to about 1.7 million, and then the same day the company said they were already at 3.3 million. That implies roughly 20% weekly growth on the recent run. I want to take that number seriously for a limited window and see where it goes relative to Waymo and to the actual ride-hail market in the Texas cities where Tesla is already operating. Then I’ll draw some conclusions.

title: Who's At Fault When Software Glitches Cause A Car Accident?
raw_summary: We're increasingly living in an era when flawed code is causing cars to break. That's according to an analysis by the group Recall Masters ' May, 2026 report. Last year the National Highway Transportation Association (NHTSA) issued a stunning 8 million recalls involving faulty electronics. Many were related to buggy back-up cameras, misfiring driver assistance systems and blipping instrument clusters. article_paragraphs: We're increasingly living in an era when flawed code is causing cars to break. That's according to an analysis by the group Recall Masters ' May, 2026 report. Last year the National Highway Transportation Association (NHTSA) issued a stunning 8 million recalls involving faulty electronics. Many were related to buggy back-up cameras, misfiring driver assistance systems and blipping instrument clusters. We don't know exactly how many fewer bricked cars this would amount to if it weren't for Ford's many recalls delaying dealer fixes, but that's a different headache.

Actually, maybe it's related. Because if any not-yet-repaired software-blipping car harmed the driver, passenger, a pedestrian or anyone else outside the vehicle, we wanted to know who'd be responsible. Is it the driver? What about the shop that made the last software patch? And, naturally, how about the car's manufacturer?

Since we're not lawyers, and are explicitly not issuing legal advice with this column, we instead asked Charles Gilman, founding attorney of the practice, Gilman of Gilman & Bedigian, LLC , with offices in Maryland, Pennsylvania and Texas. His firm has a focus on medical malpractice, but also intellectual property and automotive claims. His first answer will annoy you — but don't worry, because we didn't let him off that easily.

"This is going to depend on the glitch," he said when asked who would be at fault, "what caused the glitch, and several other factors. For example, if it's a brand new car... the issue may be a software defect, which will point to the manufacturer for liability. If it was a faulty repair or incomplete update, failure to update a known defect of the software liability will rest with the dealership or repair shop that could have [or] should have fixed it."

One question we have has to do with recalls and the responsibility of the car's driver when a recall is issued. Pity the poor Ford owner here, but not solely them. Last year Carfax said there were 54.6 million vehicles with unrepaired recalls nationwide, and this past spring they made that number a bit starker, noting that one in five vehicles on American roads has an unfixed recall. FYI, here's how you can check if your car is subject to a recall .

Now, let's say you never click on that link. Let's say you moved and never got that recall in the mail. Or, for instance, you bought a used car and don't service it at the dealer. Maybe you even do a bunch of repairs yourself, so unlike a decent independent mechanic, you're not actively searching for recalls that they would see when they rotate your tires. Really, should it be on you, the car's owner, to know if your car was designed properly? And what about the upsides and downsides of over-the-air updates ? Should you be on the hook for knowing if your slick ride is even getting those, which, theoretically, should mean fewer software glitches?

Gliman says the manufacturer probably still has more liability than you do when it comes to recalls. Put simply, just issuing a recall wouldn't by default protect the carmaker from liability in the event of an accident. "Recall notices will not necessarily release the manufacturer from claims," he says. "They may have to issue orders to stop using the vehicle depending on the defect."

Gilman can't see a scenario where a car buyer would be held at fault for purchasing the wrong car, such as one with open recalls or stop-drive orders from the manufacturer. "It would be the seller of the vehicle that should know and has the best ability to know that the vehicle should not have been sold," Gillman explains. "If the vehicle has known defects, the manufacturer and the dealership are in the best position to prevent the sale of the vehicle, so the liability should rest with them."

raw_title: These Are Your Takes On Electric Vehicles In The Face Of Expensive Gasoline
title: These Are Your Takes On Electric Vehicles In The Face Of Expensive Gasoline
raw_summary: This week I took an opportunity to visit a friend's home, and I was pleasantly surprised to discover that he'd recently purchased a used Nissan Leaf at an absolute bargain price. He reasoned that the $4,500 he spent on the car would quickly be made up by his daily local trips. He was offloading his low-mileage used AWD Dodge Charger. Rising operating costs for the Dodge, including insurance rates, oil changes, and tires (on top of mounting Stellantis maintenance bills), plus the extra set of winter tires and L2 wall charger that came with the Nissan meant the car would pay for itself in short order. This friend is a dyed-in-the-wool car nut. He has a collection of hot rods and a self-built shop space with several times more square footage than my home. When I need help tuning a carburetor or fabricating fender flares, he's the guy I call. The fact that he's been converted to the merits of electric vehicles in these trying times is, anecdotally at least, indicative of changing trends in the car market. This friend is no luddite, but he's not the sort to adopt the latest technology without good reason.

As you might suspect, the topic can be a touchy one, and the comment section was buzzing with energy.
